newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland violence ebbs but anger still burns.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland violence ebbs but anger still burns.

text.p: The flames of violent protest died down across Northern Ireland on Tuesday but anger over Protestant parades this week still burned among Catholics determined to stop marches through areas in which they live.

Security forces reported several more incidents in Belfast and elsewhere in which Catholic youths hijacked vehicles and set them ablaze, but said the violence was minor compared to the fury which engulfed the province on Sunday and early Monday.
Police were investigating the death of a Protestant youth who apparently died in an explosion in south Belfast but refused to confirm or deny speculation that he was handling a bomb.
Britain's embattled Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam issued a statement saying the circumstances surrounding his death were unclear but she added:
"One death is one death too many. Northern Ireland has seen too much tragedy. Violence solves nothing. It accomplishes nothing."

If the death was linked to guerrilla violence, it would be the first fatality since the worst violence for years engulfed Northern Ireland on Saturday after police allowed a Protestant Orange Order march through a Catholic enclave of rural Portadown.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair said he refused to bury a faltering Northern Ireland peace process sponsored by the London and Dublin governments despite predictions it had expired.
"We are going to go on searching for peace," Blair told reporters. "We will not give up, even for a moment."

Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army, appealed to youths to end the riots and car hijackings which turned Irish nationalist ghettos into no-go zones and IRA traps for police and British troops.
Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams appealed for calm and dignified protest but blamed Britain for igniting the anger that swept the 40 percent Catholic minority.

IRA guerrillas and allied groups fighting British rule of Northern Ireland put on their biggest display of firepower for years in the frenzy which followed the Portadown march on Sunday, but there were no reports of further attacks late on Monday.

Martin McGuinness, an elected member of the British parliament and Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, said he was struck by police on the head in scuffles surrounding a Catholic demonstration against a Protestant band parade in Bellaghy.

The march passed off relatively peacefully but Catholic activists said they expected massed opposition on Saturday to a parade down the Lower Ormeau Road of south Belfast, scene of violent clashes in previous years.

The parade takes place on the "Glorious Twelfth," the July 12 anniversary of a 1690 battle victory over an invading Catholic king which the Orange Order sees as one of the most cherished dates in its calendar.
Mowlam held brief talks on Monday night with leaders of the Orange Order, who are determined they will march down the road despite threats of protest by local Catholic community chiefs.
She said was hoping for "some willingness and understanding of events of this weekend reflected in their words and actions during the days ahead".

There was no immediate sign the Orange Order might agree to any rerouting of the March. Jeffrey Donaldson, assistant Grand Master of the Order, said the violence was the fault of Irish nationalists alone and said his organisation was not to blame.
"We do try to take on board legitimate concerns. But Orangemen have rights as well, enshrined in international law," he told British television.
The Order says it wants only to walk peacefully along public roads which belong to no group.

The Apprentice Boys, another Protestant civil organisation, is also planning a Saturday parade in Northern Ireland's second city of Londonderry, the birthplace of militant Irish nationalism and scene of violent protest over the weekend.
More than 100 people have been injured since Sunday, including two 14-year-old youths, one a Protestant struck by a stray bullet and the other a Catholic hit by a plastic bullet.
Mowlam told a Belfast news conference: "I understand the anger in nationalist communities, but nothing justified the orchestrated violence that we have seen in the last 24 hours."
